title: Pipelined requests hang on the second http::read
summary: A synchronous Beast client. Keep one flat_buffer per connection, stop on need_eof() and end_of_stream, and let shutdown report not_connected. Raise the 8MB body cap with body_limit on a response_parser.

turns.user: the API is slow so I write all the requests first and then read them in order. works locally but in prod the second http::read sometimes just hangs forever

assistant.body: Here's what is going on. http::read does not stop at one response. It puts whatever the socket had into the flat_buffer. With every request already sent, the next response can be waiting too, and the first read pulls its opening bytes into the buffer. The loop built a fresh buffer each time, so those bytes were thrown away, and the second read waited for data that was never coming again. Locally the responses arrived one at a time, which is why it never showed. In other words, the buffer lives as long as the connection, not the request. Build it once, outside the loop.

turns.user: no more hangs. but when the server sends Connection: close partway through, the exception throws away everything. just give me whatever came back

assistant.body: Sure. The read switches to the overload that takes an error_code, so the end of the connection is not an exception. A response carrying Connection: close has need_eof() set, and after it the loop stops reading. If the server hangs up without saying so, read returns http::error::end_of_stream, and the loop stops there too. Any other error still throws. The shutdown at the end also takes an error_code, and it is checked.

turns.user: crashed with Socket is not connected. the shutdown line

assistant.body: Apologies, my previous answer was incorrect. When the peer has already closed the connection, shutdown can report not_connected. The server closed right after its Connection: close response, which is exactly that case. The goal of the shutdown has already been met, so not_connected alone is ignored. The official Beast examples do the same.
sed -i '' 's/^  if (ec) throw beast::system_error{ec};$/  if (ec \&\& ec != beast::errc::not_connected) throw beast::system_error{ec};/' src/client/fetch.cpp

turns.user: ok. also /export is about 20MB and I get body limit exceeded. is that Beast?

assistant.body: TL;DR: yes, that is Beast. Passing a response straight to http::read uses a parser with the default limits, and a response body is capped at 8MB. To change it, build a response_parser yourself, set body_limit, and pass the parser to read. Once it is done, release() hands back the response. This sets the cap to 64MB.
